Our Story

Canvas + Crumb is Valerie Mahase's kitchen bakery: slow-fermented sourdough, painted by hand with edible color, and sold locally — one loaf at a time.

Call 917-887-2712 Why sourdough

200-year-old starter · Local pickup

The baker

Valerie Mahase

Valerie spent 23 years in the classroom, then served as a school district manager. As she eases into retirement, she has turned the patience of a long career in education toward something equally formative: bread.

About a year ago she fell hard for sourdough. What began as a kitchen experiment became a craft. She has come a long way — from first sticky doughs to loaves with an open crumb, a singing crust, and a flavor that only wild fermentation can give.

At the heart of every bake is a living heirloom: a sourdough starter more than 200 years old. Fed daily in her kitchen, it carries generations of wild yeast and bacteria into every Canvas + Crumb loaf.

Health

Why sourdough is healthier than regular bread

Commercial bread is mixed, risen, and baked in a few hours with baker's yeast. True sourdough is a food that has been transformed by time. That difference shows up in how you feel after you eat it.

Naturally fermented

Wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria work for many hours, breaking down gluten and phytic acid so minerals like iron, zinc, and magnesium are easier to absorb.

Gentler on digestion

The long ferment pre-digests starches and proteins. Many people who feel heavy after commercial bread find true sourdough easier to eat.

Lower glycemic impact

Organic acids slow starch digestion, so blood sugar rises more steadily than with yeasted supermarket loaves packed with added sugar.

No shortcuts, no additives

Flour, water, salt, and time. No dough conditioners, no preservatives, no industrial yeast — just a living culture and a hot oven.

A 200-year-old culture in every slice

An ancient starter is not a marketing flourish. Decades — in this case, centuries — of continuous feeding select a stable community of microbes. That culture is what gives Valerie's bread its tang, its keeping quality, and its distinctive aroma. You cannot replicate it with a packet of instant yeast.

Why it costs more

You are not paying for bread. You are paying for time.

A supermarket loaf is engineered for speed and shelf life. Flour is mixed with commercial yeast, enzymes, and conditioners so it can be baked, bagged, and shipped in a single shift.

Valerie's loaves take the better part of two days. The dough ferments slowly, is folded by hand, proofed until it is ready — not until a timer says so — and baked in small batches from her own kitchen. There is no factory, no night shift, no bulk discount on flavor.

You pay more because the ingredients are simple and the labor is not. You pay for a 200-year-old starter, for stone-ground flour, for the hours she cannot rush, and for bread that is food rather than filler. A loaf that keeps, toasts beautifully, and actually nourishes is cheaper by the week than bread you throw away.

Canvas, then crumb

Edible paint, seasonal flair

Valerie treats the crust as a canvas. Using food-safe, edible paints, she scores and paints each loaf with seasonal motifs or a stylistic flourish — autumn leaves, winter botanicals, a simple gold wash for a celebration.

The paint is meant to be eaten. It is a thin, flavor-neutral layer that bakes onto the crust, so the loaf is as welcome on a holiday table as it is sliced for Tuesday toast. No two painted loaves are identical.

Ask when you order: Valerie can match a season, a color story, or a quiet unpainted loaf if you prefer the crust au naturel.

From the kitchen

Real sourdough — blistered crusts, open crumb, and the kind of aroma that fills a house.
